title: The nurse
hookLine: during the Civil War, Whitman went ward to ward in the military hospitals (Specimen Days)
tomorrow: what small creature did Dickinson say lives in the soul?

lines: A BALLOON IN THE GIFT SHOP.
cards: Someone you love is in the hospital, and you're standing in the gift shop holding a balloon, wondering what actually helps. Whitman had his version.
Word came that his brother George had been wounded in the war, and Whitman went south to find him. The wound turned out to be slight. But Whitman didn't go home.
He stayed in the capital and began going to the military hospitals, ward after ward, day after day.

teach.h: WHAT DO YOU BRING THE SICK?
teach.b: So today's question: what do you bring to someone who's sick?

In his notes, later gathered as Specimen Days, Whitman lists small things: fruit, writing paper and envelopes, a little money, a book. He wrote letters home for young men who couldn't. He sat by beds.
And he wrote that the visits themselves, a friendly presence, seemed to help as much as anything he carried.
His poem The Wound-Dresser says it plainly: "Bearing the bandages, water and sponge, Straight and swift to my wounded I go." That's Whitman's answer: bring yourself, and stay. Now a neighbor's words.

teach.h: MATTHEW: I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED.
teach.b: In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus tells of a king who welcomes the righteous, and among the reasons: "I was sick, and ye visited me."

When they ask when, he answers: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." Matthew and Whitman share the act itself: go to the bedside, and don't send a substitute.
The honest difference is the why.
In Matthew, the one who visits the sick meets Christ in them. Whitman gives no such reason. He calls them "my wounded," and goes because they're there.

how: Visiting the sick is honored on many paths; some people on this one bring something small, offer to write or read for the person, and mostly sit and stay.

games.q: a friend's dad is in the hospital, and you barely know him. you're unsure you'd be welcome. what fits Whitman and Matthew?
o: ask your friend if you can come by, then go, bring something small, and stay a bit.
send a big bouquet and stay away, so you don't intrude.
wait to visit until you know exactly the right thing to say.
games.why: both put the visit itself first. Whitman's gifts were small; the presence was the point.

practice: Bring to mind someone who's ill or stuck at home. If you can, send them a short message now, nothing to fix, just: thinking of you, can I come by?
If a message isn't right, choose the day you'll visit, and hold that plan for a minute.

wordCard.voice: The nurse: Whitman in the war hospitals, untrained, just there, ward after ward, with paper, fruit and his own presence. Bring yourself, and stay.

carryVoice: Keep this: the visitor. The gift is showing up, and staying a while by the bed. See you tomorrow.
